The sea tadpole Careproctus reinhardti is a liparid fish inhabiting cold Arctic and North Atlantic waters, where individuals experience stable thermal conditions near 3 °C [T = 3 °C]. Under these frigid temperatures, newly hatched prolarvae emerge from the chorion after an incubation period of approximately 55 days [ab = approximately 55 days] at a temperature of 3 °C [T = 3 °C]. These yolk-sac larvae possess a wet weight at birth of just 0.033 grams [Wwb = 0.033 grams], an extremely low mass relative to the species' eventual adult body size. The protracted hatching interval reflects the profoundly retarded metabolic rates characteristic of polar fishes, wherein enzymatic processes operate slowly under near-freezing conditions. Initial growth proceeds entirely through endogenous yolk reserves before the mouth gapes and exogenous feeding begins, a phase that imposes a critical bottleneck on early survival.

As the endotrophic larvae exhaust their yolk reserves, they transition to active feeding and begin accumulating somatic tissue across the prolonged juvenile phase. Studies indicate that at a water temperature of 3 °C [T = 3 °C], individuals attain total length at puberty of 12 centimeters [Lp = 12 centimeters], corresponding to a wet weight at puberty of approximately 11.8 grams [Wwp = approximately 11.8 grams]. The puberty length–mass relationship follows the allometric equation derived from adult body proportions, with the mass exponent reflecting a moderately elongate body form typical of benthic liparids. This size at reproductive maturation is modest compared to the ultimate total length of 30 centimeters [Li = 30 centimeters] and the ultimate wet weight of 215 grams [Wwi = 215 grams] that individuals can achieve later in life. The considerable post-pubertal growth window suggests a life-history strategy in which reproduction begins well before somatic growth is complete, a pattern documented in several other deep-sea and cold-water teleosts.

Reproductive output in Careproctus reinhardti has been characterised from captive observations. Gravid females deposit demersal, adhesive eggs in clutches, with a maximum daily reproductive rate of approximately 0.68 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 0.68 eggs per day] at 3 °C [T = 3 °C]. This daily rate is derived from a maximum annual output of roughly 250 eggs per year, with the spawning period extending throughout the entire year. The low per-day fecundity reflects both the large egg diameter of 4 millimeters — which necessitates substantial maternal investment per offspring — and the cold temperatures that constrain vitellogenic rates. The trade-off between egg size and fecundity is typical of liparids inhabiting food-limited environments.

Longevity records for the sea tadpole derive primarily from field mark-recapture studies conducted in subzero habitats. The oldest documented individual reached a lifespan of 2,920 days [am = 2,920 days] at 3 °C [T = 3 °C], a duration equivalent to 8 years. This considerable longevity, exceeding that of many shallow-water teleosts of comparable body size, is consistent with the metabolic theory of ecology, which predicts extended lifespans under low temperature regimes where rates of oxidative damage accumulation are diminished. It is noteworthy, however, that length-at-age data from FishBase indicate that individuals attaining such advanced ages rarely exceed 20 centimeters, suggesting that the asymptotic structural length of 30 cm [Li = 30 cm] is typically reserved for faster-growing individuals under optimal feeding conditions.

Comparative analyses with confamilial liparids highlight several unusual features in the life history of Careproctus reinhardti. While many shallow-water congeners complete their entire life cycle within one to two years, this species delays first reproduction until after reaching a body mass of at least 11.8 grams [Wwp = 11.8 grams] at puberty, and the neonatal wet weight of 0.033 grams [Wwb = 0.033 grams] is among the smallest recorded for any Arctic liparid. The large egg diameter — the basis for the high per-offspring investment — contrasts with the fecundity of similarly sized Scorpaeniformes, which often produce numerous small pelagic eggs. Furthermore, given that the maximum daily reproductive rate of approximately 0.68 eggs [Ri = daily reproductive rate of approximately 0.68 eggs] is sustained across the entire year at 3 °C [T = 3 °C], the spawning strategy appears to involve continuous or prolonged batch spawning, an adaptation to unpredictable food availability in polar waters.
